title: The Climb
enemy_damage_note:
What a kind of enemy HITS FOR on this level, overriding the damage in its profile (features/combat/enemy.gd). Applied at spawn by _build_world in game/session.gd, by kind, exactly as enemy_health is. Only the plain swing: a special keeps the number in its own move data.

The bandit's 20 is tuned for flat ground, where a hit costs a fifth of the bar and you back off and come again. There is no backing off here. The one bandit on this mountain stands at 156, -1116 on a shelf with nothing either side of it, and his committed 215 px/s dash lands with a knockback that carries the player off the ledge rather than across it - so his blow is not worth a fifth of the bar, it is worth the whole band of climbing below it. 12 is that hit at three-fifths, which leaves him something to say at arm's length while making the fall, not the damage, the thing that ends a run.

The five hunters are NOT listed here and keep their 14 and their arrow's 12. An arrow is the fight this level is actually about - it is the only thing that reaches a climber who is committed and in the air - and turning it down is turning down the mountain. See enemies_note.
tagline: The only way off it is up.
brief: 47 jumps up a mountain of torn-off isles.
scope: A mountain, not a course. The camera does not travel sideways at all - the level is exactly one screen wide, so the whole column is in shot and every jump is read rather than discovered. What moves is the view going up, and it only goes up. 47 hops and 3856 px of it, which is a little over seven screens stacked end to end.
climb_note: The one key that makes this a climb. It does two things, both in game/session.gd: the view ratchets, rising as he lands higher and never coming back down, and the fatal line rides with it at CLIMB_DROP below the highest ledge he has stood on instead of sitting at fall_y. So falling off the bottom of the screen is what kills him. That is the whole level: there is no floor under any of this, and the sea is only the backstop for the first few jumps. It is also what keeps a mountain this tall playable - a miss near the summit would otherwise be nine seconds of watching him drop past everything he had already beaten.
width_note: One viewport exactly. session.gd clamps the camera to half a viewport from either end, so at this width there is nothing left for it to do horizontally and it pins at x 480 for the whole level. That is deliberate and the design rests on it - a mountain you can see the whole width of, however far up it you are.
sea_drift_note: How much of the climb the waterline comes up with him, in features/world/scenery.gd. Every other level leaves this at 1.0 and keeps the sea at a fixed height on screen, which is right for a course along a coast and wrong for one that goes up. At 0.85 the sea gives back 15 percent of whatever he gains, and on a climb this long that is what draws the bands: the sea is in frame for the first 1800 px, the cloud bank sits across the middle of it, and the last thousand is open sky with nothing in it but the rock hanging over him. Tuned to the height - at the 0.72 a shorter version used, the sea was gone before he was a third of the way up.
solids_note: [x, top_y, w, h] and an optional fifth value naming the art it wears. The named ones are the floating land masses out of the Magic Cliffs pack, drawn centred on the rectangle with their standable surface on its top edge, so what you see is exactly what you land on. Their h is 18 and nothing more: the collision is a lip, and the art hangs 30 to 55 px below it with nothing behind it. Which piece is a band's is the level's treeline - island_large is grassed, island_wide and rock_float are bare stone, so the mountain loses its greenery on the way up without one line of decor saying it does. The shore and the summit name no art and get the procedural cliff, which is what makes them read as the only two pieces of real ground in the level.
geometry_note: 47 hops, 3856 px of climb, and every one measured against the envelope in features/player/tuning.gd before it was written down. The jump apex is 106.7, so no step may rise more than that and none here rises more than 92. Seven bands, and both the rise and the gap grow through them while the ledges narrow - 68 px steps onto 72 px islands at the bottom, 92 px steps onto 36 px rocks at the top. The widest gap is 120 px and the tightest hop in the level is 74 percent of what a full-speed jump reaches there, inside the 80 the validator warns at. The switchbacks are not authored: the layout marches until the next ledge would leave the column and turns where it has to, which is what keeps every flight the full width of the screen.
gates_note: Deliberately none. A gate is a vertical wall at an x, and in a column one screen wide that is a wall across the whole level. Nothing here holds him anywhere; the climb is its own gate, because the only way back down is the one that kills him.
hazards_note: None, and there is no room for any. Spikes are for a level with a floor. Everything dangerous here is either the drop or something falling down it.
rockfall_note: [x, y, every, first]: a stone leaves (x, y) every `every` seconds, the first one `first` seconds in, and falls straight down until it meets a ledge, the player or the sea. 21 sources, hung over 31 of the 47 jumps. Each one is placed in the lane above a jump, 300 px up, and only where that lane is actually open - a source with a ledge under it drops a stone that breaks before it reaches anyone, which is silent in play and looks like a shaft that simply does not work. A source only drops while he is below it and inside ROCKFALL_REACH, about a screen, so a mountain this tall only ever has three or four of them live at once and each band wakes as he climbs into it.
rockfall_design_note: Nothing about it is random, and that is the point: a shaft learned on one attempt behaves identically on the next, which is the only thing that makes a climb this long worth retrying. A stone does 18 of his 100 and stuns him for a quarter of a second, which matters far less than where it catches him - the stun zeroes his movement input, so one taken mid-jump drops him straight out of the arc, and over this level there is nothing underneath. He can also punch or blast one out of the air; see take_hit in features/combat/stone.gd.
crates_note: Rocks: breakable, liftable, throwable, [x, ground_y]. Two on the shore, which is the only place with room to experiment with one, and three more on wide ledges beside the things worth throwing one at. Carrying one is a real decision here - it is two-handed and it slows him down, on a level that is nothing but jumps.
bottles_note: Milk, [x, ground_y, bars]. Four, spread up the mountain roughly a band apart, because the climb is long enough that a full bar at the bottom is not a full bar at the top and the stones will have had several goes at him by then.
brews_note: The brown bottle, against the mana bar. Two, on wide ledges at the foot of the bands with the most rock coming down them - which is where blasting a stone out of the air instead of dodging it starts being worth the mana.
enemies_note: [x, ground_y, kind]. One per shelf and one on the summit, and FIVE OF THE EIGHT ARE HUNTERS, which is the difference between holding a mountain and holding a corridor. An archer aims at where the player actually is rather than along his own facing, so he is the only enemy here that can do anything at all about someone who is below him and out of arm's reach, which on this level is almost everyone almost all of the time. A bandit on a shelf 400 px over his head is scenery until he arrives. Where an archer can REACH is worth knowing before placing one, and tests/diag_ratchet.gd sweeps it and prints the map. The arrow leaves 34 px above his feet, so a steep shot downward crosses the top of the very ledge he is standing on and buries itself in it a few pixels later: he cannot shoot straight down past his own lip. What he covers is his own height and about one ledge below it - which is exactly the approach to his shelf, the last two jumps of a band, when the player is committed and in the air. Below that he is quiet, and the mountain is its own cover the rest of the time, because every ledge is solid and stops an arrow. NOTHING STANDS ON A SWITCHBACK LEDGE, though the turn fix left them 72 to 96 wide and they are the obvious place for three more bows. Three were tried there and they are a wall rather than a fight: a corner is the one ledge he lands on running one way and has to leave going the other, he has about 36 px to turn around in, and a stun there costs him the only run-up he gets. A climber who would not stop to fight went from finishing the mountain with no deaths at all to dying sixteen times on the same corner and never passing ledge 19. The same reason the corners were widened is the reason they stay empty. One bandit and two marks are kept for the contrast: something that has to be fought at arm's length, on a ledge with nothing either side of it, is a different problem from something shooting at him while he jumps. All eight can be climbed past, and the mark on the summit is the last thing between the climb and the way out.
signs_note: None, the same as The Fractured Isles. There is nothing here to introduce - the jump and the drop are both taught in First Steps - and the one thing this level does differently explains itself the first time the screen refuses to come back down.
decor_note: [x, bottom_y, piece]. Deliberately NO floating island art in here as decoration. Every other level can afford a rock drifting in the background; this one cannot, because scenery.gd draws decor at the same visual depth as the terrain and a painted ledge you cannot stand on would be a death in a level where every death is a fall. Everything a player could mistake for a platform here IS one. The only thing dressed into the open sky is the rock_mass slab over each shaft, and it is the only thing that CAN be: rock_mass is a silhouette scenery.gd draws itself, so it has a real outline. Every hanging sprite in the pack is a square tile with the cave-rock fill painted right out to its edges - vine is 32x32 with not one transparent pixel in it, vine_rock and hang_thin are 8 and 3 percent clear - so they only work laid against a cliff face, which is what the other levels do with them. Ten vines were hung down an earlier version of this tower and every one rendered as a black box nailed to the sky. The plants stop at y 200, which is this mountain's treeline.
ground_note: The Fractured Isles' numbers, with the two that shape a cliff face changed, so the shore at the bottom of this mountain is visibly the same coast he left and the summit is not a black rectangle hanging in the sky. The Isles leans 0.15 and only lets a cliff lean at all past 408 px wide, which is right for a coastline: there the cliffs are long and their faces run down out of shot. Both pieces of real ground here are islands visible all the way round, and the summit is 216 wide - under that 408 - so it drew as a flat slab with two hard bottom corners. At lean 0.5 from 200 px up it closes to a wedge instead, which is what torn-off land looks like from underneath.

cutscene.caption: Its running away! I need to follow it and only way off these floating isles is up.

cutscene_note:
One establishing card, and the only level that opens on one. `at` is an x and _story_due in game/session.gd fires the first card whose x he has reached while he is ON HIS FEET, so 0 means the frame the level starts: spawn is x=140 and he is standing on it. That is the point of this picture rather than a walk-in like The Dragon's Roost's - the shot IS the level brief, the column of islands going up out of frame with him at the foot of it, and it has to land before he has begun rather than after he has already seen the first three shelves for himself.

A climb is also the one level where a walk-in could not work: `at` is compared against x, this level is 960 wide and goes UP, so there is no run of x to place a cue along. 0 is not a shortcut here, it is the only position that means anything.

Two clips, the same split The Fractured Isles' first card uses. `audio` is the narration over the picture and `out_audio` is what REPLACES it as the card dissolves - see _begin_story_out in game/session.gd, where the tail cuts in over the level rather than under the panel. So the line is heard against the still and the dragon is heard against the climb it is about to leave him to, which is the right way round: the picture is what he is being told, the dragon is where he is going.

`out_audio` is dragon_fight_end, the clip the isles' departure card plays - the dragon on the wing, which is what is in the top-left of this picture and what the line is about. Shared between two cards on purpose; nothing binds a clip to one panel.

There is deliberately NO pinned `hold`: _read_story_card takes the hold off `audio` when there is one, so the card is as long as the narration and re-rendering it retunes the card to match. That is 4.83 s of narration, a 4.13 s hold and 5.43 s on screen once the 0.7 in and 0.6 out are counted. The tail is 9.53 s and deliberately OUTLASTS the card - it is meant to still be going while he takes his first steps up. Pin a `hold` only to shorten the picture; a pin under the narration cuts the line off mid-sentence.

`skip` false, as on every story card in the game: the picture is short and it is the whole of this level's setup.
brief_note: Kept under about 66 characters on purpose. The menu draws this on a fixed card through wrapped() in ui/hud.gd, which is capped at two lines, and anything past them is simply not drawn - the sentence stops mid-thought with no sign that it did.
